q: What is a development approach, according to the Standard?
options: A stage of the life cycle in which deliverables are built and tested
The means used to create and evolve the product, service or result
The order in which the project's phases are approved by the sponsor
A list of the processes every project must follow
explanation: A development approach is the means used to create and evolve a product, service or result during the life cycle, such as predictive, adaptive or hybrid. The development phase is a stage of the life cycle, a different thing.

q: At a phase gate, which of these is a possible decision according to the Standard?
options: Skip the review, because the project is on schedule
Approve the next phase without comparing performance
Park the project temporarily for an urgent initiative
Restart the whole project from initiation automatically
explanation: After comparing performance with the documents that specify expectations, the decision may be to continue, continue with modification, end the project or phase, remain in the phase, repeat it or parts of it, or park the project temporarily for another urgent initiative.

q: How do risk, uncertainty and the cost of changes typically develop over a project's life?
options: Risk and uncertainty fall while the cost of changes rises
Risk and uncertainty rise while the cost of changes falls
All three stay roughly the same throughout the project
All three are highest at closure, when acceptance happens
explanation: Figure 4-1 shows risk and uncertainty decreasing and the cost of changes increasing over project time. Stakeholders' ability to influence scope cheaply is often highest at the start.

q: For which of these is a predictive approach most likely to be optimal?
options: A new mobile app whose features depend on market reaction
A research project exploring a new business model
A digital service whose scope keeps evolving with users
The build phase of a building whose design is approved
explanation: A predictive approach may be optimal when scope can be stabilized early, and for projects or phases in which the cost of iterating far exceeds its value, such as the build phase of many construction projects.

q: In an incremental predictive approach, what stays largely fixed?
options: The overall scope and timeline
The order of each sprint's backlog
The size of each iteration's team
The product vision, but not the scope
explanation: In an incremental predictive approach the scope is understood and planned up front but delivered in phases or increments; stakeholder value comes earlier, while the overall scope and timeline remain largely fixed.

q: In the Standard's description of agile methods, how long are iterations generally?
options: 1 to 4 days
1 to 4 weeks
1 to 4 months
6 to 12 months
explanation: Some agile methods entail iterations of generally 1 to 4 weeks, with a demonstration of the accomplishments at the end of each iteration.

q: What does an iterative approach focus on, as opposed to an incremental one?
options: Delivering the product in small usable segments that build on one another
Planning the whole scope in detail before any work begins
Refining and improving the product through repeated cycles
Releasing a single complete product at the very end
explanation: The iterative approach refines and improves through repeated cycles; the incremental approach delivers the product in small usable segments that each provide value. Adaptive approaches can be both.

q: Which of these does the Standard describe as a tool kit rather than a method?
options: Disciplined Agile
Scrum
Extreme Programming
Kanban
explanation: A method is a systematic way of doing something; a tool kit is a collection of tools and techniques to choose from. PMI Disciplined Agile is designed to be a tool kit.

q: What does the Eighth Edition say about hybrid approaches in practice?
options: They should be avoided, because they confuse the team and the sponsor
They are only allowed when the sponsor requests them
They are suitable only for construction projects
Most projects can strongly benefit from a hybrid approach
explanation: In practice, most projects can strongly benefit from a hybrid approach: it gives flexibility to adapt to changing conditions while keeping control over predictable aspects.

q: A company develops a new high-tech product in agile iterations; then a separate team rolls it out and trains thousands of users to a fixed plan. Which hybrid pattern is this?
options: Predictive development followed by an adaptive rollout
Adaptive development followed by a predictive rollout
A largely adaptive approach with no predictive part
Predictive and adaptive used side by side by one team
explanation: Adaptive development followed by a predictive rollout suits work with uncertainty in development and a defined, repeatable rollout, perhaps by a different team, such as a high-tech product followed by training for thousands of users.

q: On the Stacey matrix, both the requirements and the technology are certain. What does the Agile Practice Guide suggest?
options: Predictive approaches work well here
Only crisis methods will work here
An exploratory approach is essential
The project should not start yet
explanation: In the lower-left corner of the Stacey matrix, where requirements and technology are both certain, traditional predictive approaches work well. As either becomes uncertain, adaptive or exploratory life cycles help.

q: In the Cynefin Framework's complex domain, what approach does the Agile Practice Guide recommend?
options: Sense, categorize, respond
Act, sense, respond
Probe, sense, respond
Analyze, plan, execute
explanation: In the complex domain, outcomes emerge through experimentation, so the recommended approach is probe, sense and respond, which aligns with agile short feedback cycles and iterative delivery.

q: Why does a critical nuclear reactor project need more rigor than a new office building, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Because predictive projects always need more documents
Because offices are built only with adaptive approaches
Because the sponsor of a reactor project always prefers much longer reports
Because criticality and scale change how much rigor is needed
explanation: Tailoring considers criticality, scale, duration, complexity, industry standards and other variables. The rigor, checks and reporting for a critical nuclear reactor project are much greater than for an office building.

q: A team must build something using a new technology and a new business model. Which approach does the Standard suggest may be optimal?
options: Predictive
Adaptive
Single delivery
Waterfall
explanation: Degree of innovation: when new or complex technological or business model innovation is needed, an adaptive approach may be optimal.

q: Why do products with rigorous safety requirements often use a predictive approach?
options: Significant up-front planning is needed to ensure safety compliance
Safety-critical products never change in any way after the first iteration
Agile teams are not allowed to work on safety products
Predictive projects do not need any testing at all
explanation: Products that have rigorous safety requirements often use a predictive approach, as there is a need for significant up-front planning to ensure safety compliance.

q: What team size do some adaptive frameworks recommend, according to the Standard?
options: One to two members
Ten to twenty members
Three to nine members
Twenty or more
explanation: Adaptive approaches often work better with smaller teams; some adaptive frameworks recommend between three and nine team members.

q: An organization has a strong culture of managing and directing, with progress measured against baselines. What does the Standard say?
options: Adaptive approaches will fit best without any change
The organization's culture is not relevant to the choice
No project in this organization can be tailored
A predictive approach may be the better fit here
explanation: A predictive approach may fit better in a culture of managing and directing, where work is planned and progress measured against baselines. Adaptive approaches fit cultures that embrace uncertainty and self-managed teams.

q: A new project team wants a structured way to weigh its culture, team and project factors before choosing a predictive, adaptive or hybrid approach. Which tool does the PMBOK Guide describe for this?
options: A suitability filter
A responsibility assignment matrix
An iteration burndown chart
A stakeholder register
explanation: A suitability filter is a decision-making tool, not a rigid procedure, that evaluates culture, team and project factors to help decide on the initial approach, combined with other data.

q: A software team delivers internally every two weeks, on a fixed schedule, and releases to the market periodically. Which delivery cadence is this?
options: Single delivery
Periodic deliveries
Continuous delivery
Multiple deliveries
explanation: Periodic deliveries are like multiple deliveries but on a regular, fixed schedule, such as internal deliveries every 2 weeks with periodic market releases.

q: A process reengineering project rolls out its new process only near the end. Which delivery cadence is this?
options: Continuous delivery
Periodic deliveries
Single delivery
Multiple deliveries
explanation: Projects with a single delivery produce all outcomes at the end, for example a process-reengineering project with no deliveries until the new process is rolled out.

q: What does the PMBOK Guide say about using more processes than a project requires?
options: It always improves the chance of project success
It is required for every project above a certain size
It is the safest choice for an adaptive team
It is costly and wasteful, as too few are ineffective
explanation: Too few processes can lead to ineffective project management, while employing more processes than required is costly and wasteful. Tailoring leads to optimum and effective project management.

q: In process tailoring, which action reduces unnecessary cost or effort?
options: Removing elements
Adding elements
Aligning elements
Blending elements
explanation: Process tailoring adds elements for unique conditions or rigor, modifies them to fit, removes them to reduce unnecessary cost or effort, blends them for added value, and aligns them for consistency.

q: When is tailoring done, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Once, when the project charter is approved, and never again after that
Only at the end, as part of the lessons learned
Continually: review points, gates and retrospectives refine it
Only when the sponsor requests a new methodology
explanation: Tailoring is not a single, one-time exercise. Review points, phase gates and retrospectives all provide opportunities to inspect and adapt the process, development approach and delivery frequency.

q: Which THREE factors point toward a predictive approach, according to the Standard?
options: Rigorous safety requirements
Significant regulatory oversight
Changes that are difficult or costly to make
A high degree of innovation
Much value from frequent feedback
Financing uncertainty
explanation: Safety requirements, regulation and costly change point toward predictive. Innovation, value from frequent feedback and financing uncertainty point toward adaptive or iterative approaches.

q: Which TWO factors point toward an adaptive approach, according to the Standard?
options: Unstable scope
Value from delivering something early
Well-known, straightforward requirements
A fixed functional hierarchy
Rigorous safety requirements
explanation: The less stable the scope, the more optimal an adaptive approach; if there is value in delivering something early, an iterative or adaptive approach may be optimal. Known requirements, functional hierarchies and safety point toward predictive.

q: Which TWO are steps of the tailoring process in the PMBOK Guide?
options: Tailor for the organization
Implement ongoing improvement
Freeze the approach at initiation
Remove principles that do not apply
Copy the previous project's approach
explanation: The four steps are: select the initial development approach, tailor for the organization, tailor for the project, and implement ongoing improvement.

q: Match each Cynefin domain with its description.
right: Cause and effect are obvious; good practices apply
Expert analysis is needed; outcomes are predictable
Outcomes emerge through experimentation and learning
Immediate action is needed to stabilize the situation
explanation: The Cynefin Framework's domains are simple, complicated, complex, chaotic and disorder. In the complex domain, probe, sense and respond; in the complicated domain, analysis may work, possibly with a hybrid life cycle.

q: Which development approach should the project manager recommend for the warehouse?
options: Predictive for everything, since there is a fixed 12-month target
Hybrid: predictive installation and inspection, adaptive software
Adaptive for everything, since part of the solution is uncertain
No approach until all software requirements are fully known
explanation: The installation and inspection are well defined, costly to change and regulated (predictive), while the routing software is uncertain and benefits from feedback (adaptive). Several approaches may be used in one project for different deliverables.

q: How should the routing software be developed?
options: Fully specified first, then built in one release before opening
By the contractor, as part of the fixed installation contract
Postponed until after the warehouse has opened for business
In short iterations, with feedback from operations trials
explanation: Requirements that are still being discovered and much value from frequent feedback point to an adaptive approach: short iterations with early trials, refining the software as the operations team learns.

q: Where does the fire-safety inspection fit best in the life cycle?
options: In every iteration of the software, as a sprint review item
After opening, once the warehouse is already running
As a planned gate before opening, with up-front planning
Nowhere, because the contractor is responsible for safety
explanation: Safety and regulatory requirements favor up-front planning, and phase gates review exit criteria before proceeding; the inspection belongs as a planned checkpoint before the warehouse opens.
